FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Discuss the presentation of, workup for, and treatment modalities for soft-tissue sarcomas.
Identify soft-tissue sarcomas that can spread through lymphatics.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Sarcomas are malignant soft-tissue masses that arise from connective tissues (muscle, fat,
neural, and vascular).
Sarcomas are rare (ratio of benign to malignant soft-tissue masses is 100:1).
Two major categories: sarcomas with a pathognomonic gene alteration and sarcomas with
disparate and complex genomic profiles

The appearance of most sarcomas on MRI is nonspecific; biopsy is required for diagnosis.
Staging—The most common staging system is the American Joint Committee on Cancer
system, which relies on tumor size, tumor grade, lymph node status, and whether distant
metastases are present.
Epidemiology
Males are affected more commonly than females.
60% of sarcomas affect the extremities (lower extremities affected more than the upper
extremities).
85% occur in individuals older than 15 years.
Risk Factors
History of radiation therapy may predispose individuals to soft-tissue sarcoma.
Angiosarcoma can arise in the setting of lymphedema.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Commonly presents as a painless, enlarging mass
Rapid growth typically, but not always, indicates higher grade.
Physical Examination
Palpation may help to distinguish superficial versus deep tumors.
The locoregional lymph nodes also should be palpated.
Neurovascular Examination
A neurovascular examination of the affected extremity should be performed.
Mass effect of the tumor may compress the nerves or blood vessels in the area; less
commonly, the neurovascular structures may be encased in the tumor.
Imaging Studies

Radiography
Plain radiographs may demonstrate a soft-tissue shadow suggestive of a mass or, less
commonly, mineralization (such as the calcifications in synovial sarcoma).
Computed Tomography
Most sarcoma metastases first occur in the lungs; therefore, chest CT is necessary for staging
and surveillance.
Imaging of the chest/abdomen/pelvis is indicated for patients diagnosed with myxoid
liposarcoma.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Sarcomas typically grow centrifugally and compress surrounding structures instead of
infiltrating/enveloping them.
Sarcomas typically are hypointense on T1-weighted MRIs, hyperintense on T2-weighted MRIs,
and variably enhance depending on the amount of necrosis.
Positron Emission Tomography
Synovial sarcoma, clear cell sarcoma, angiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and epithelioid
sarcoma tend to spread through the lymphatics; positron emission tomography may be useful
in these subtypes.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is based on core needle or open biopsy.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Radiation Therapy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Sarcomas
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000517
3/10

Radiation therapy is used routinely as an adjuvant to surgical management of high-grade soft-
tissue sarcoma. It targets microscopic residual disease, improving local control and allowing
for closer surgical margins. This allows for less morbid resections and more frequent limb
salvage.
Noted exceptions to the use of radiation therapy are if an amputation is performed or if the
sarcoma is small, superficial, low grade, or amenable to wide surgical resection.
Radiation therapy most often is administered via external beam techniques (photons or
protons). Some centers have options for intraoperative radiation to boost the total dose at an
area of concern.
Early radiation therapy effects: desquamation, delayed wound healing (Figure 1), and
infection. Late radiation therapy effects: fibrosis, fractures (Figure 2), joint stiffness, and
secondary sarcoma (depending on treatment dose, volume, and length of follow-up).
Figure 1 Clinical photograph shows wound breakdown in a patient who underwent
preoperative radiation therapy and surgical resection of a high-grade liposarcoma of the
medial thigh. (Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant soft-tissue tumors, in Lieberman JR, ed:
AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1605-1618.)

Figure 2 Images of the right distal femur of a 64-year-old woman who was treated via 50 Gy of
preoperative radiation therapy for a large, high-grade posterior thigh sarcoma 5 years ago with
periosteal stripping of 70% of the femur. A, Sagittal T2-weighted MRI shows marrow changes
and a nondisplaced fracture (arrow) along the posterior cortex in the distal diaphysis. B,
Lateral radiograph obtained 1 week later demonstrates an angulated post-radiation femur
fracture. The patient underwent femoral stabilization with the use of an intramedullary nail.
(Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant soft-tissue tumors, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 1605-1618.)
Preoperative radiation requires a lower dose (approximately 50 Gy) than postoperative
radiation (approximately 66 Gy), decreases the surrounding edema, and helps form a fibrous
capsule around the tumor. Surgical management is delayed 4 to 6 weeks after completion of
radiation therapy.
Preoperative radiation therapy incurs a higher early wound complication rate (35%) than
postoperative radiation therapy (17%). Conversely, postoperative radiation therapy leads to
more fibrosis and stiffness late.

No difference in local recurrence or overall survival is related to the timing of radiation
therapy.
External beam radiation therapy (dose-related) combined with extensive periosteal stripping
during tumor resection increases the risk of post-radiation therapy fracture. In these cases,
immediate or delayed prophylactic intramedullary or plate stabilization should be considered.
If positive microscopic margins are observed after surgical resection, no evidence shows that
an additional radiation therapy boost decreases local recurrence.
Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy is part of the standard of care for rhabdomyosarcoma and soft-tissue Ewing
sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor.
For most other types of localized soft-tissue sarcoma, limited evidence supports
chemotherapy benefit. Studies show some effect on local or systemic disease recurrence but
an equivocal difference in survival.1
Given the elevated risk of metastasis in high-grade, large soft-tissue sarcomas, chemotherapy
frequently is offered, often in a clinical trial setting. Patients with metastatic disease often
undergo systemic therapy to prolong survival.
Common agents include ifosfamide and doxorubicin, which have considerable toxicity in high
doses. Taxanes can be used for angiosarcoma. Gemcitabine and docetaxel are used for
leiomyosarcoma.
Patients with soft-tissue sarcoma who are older and have more comorbidities often cannot
tolerate high-dose systemic treatment.
Recent clinical trials on targeted therapies, immunotherapy, and chimeric antigen receptor T-
cell therapies show incremental progress in the management of various sarcoma subtypes.
Surgical Management
The goal of surgical management is to achieve an acceptable margin to minimize local
recurrence and maintain reasonable function.
Limb salvage procedures are performed in approximately 90% of patients.
A reactive zone around the tumor includes edema, fibrous tissue (capsule), inflammatory cells,
and tumor cells. This should be excised en bloc with the tumor and/or undergo radiation
therapy to prevent local recurrence. Surgical margins were defined according to Enneking et
al:2

Intralesional: resection through the tumor mass for gross total resection
Marginal: resection through the reactive zone
Wide: resection with a cuff of normal tissue
Radical: resection of the entire compartment (eg, quadriceps)
Indications
Indications for limb salvage
Limb salvage is possible in most patients.
Limb-sparing surgery is indicated if the tumor can be resected with negative margins with
function that is better than amputation.
Local recurrence does not clearly affect overall survival in patients with soft-tissue sarcoma;
therefore, close but negative margins may be accepted around vital structures.
Indications for amputation
If necessary, to resect the entire tumor in potentially curative (nonmetastatic) cases
If critical structures (nerves, vessels, bones, and soft tissue) cannot be saved, resulting in
unacceptably high complication risks and/or a poorly functioning limb
In some locally recurrent sarcomas
If the patient has considerable comorbidities that preclude limb-sparing surgery
Surgical Approaches
Standard oncologic techniques are used to resect soft-tissue sarcomas, including the use of a
tourniquet without exsanguination; excision of any open biopsy tract (not considered
imperative in patients undergoing percutaneous needle biopsy if radiation therapy is used for
local control); and use of drains distal, close, and in line with the incision such that the tract
can be excised if recurrence occurs along the drain.
Surgical resection alone of large, deep, or high-grade tumors is associated with an
unacceptably high rate of local recurrence and requires adjuvant treatment (radiation therapy
with or without chemotherapy).
Soft-tissue reconstruction via free or rotational tissue transfer often is necessary; it minimizes
wound complications after major resection, especially if preoperative radiation therapy is used
(Figure 3).

Figure 3 Clinical photographs of the wrist of a patient who underwent soft-tissue sarcoma
resection. A, Soft-tissue defect after wide resection of a clear cell sarcoma of the volar wrist. B,
Soft- tissue reconstruction via free tissue transfer. This procedure is commonly performed to
minimize wound breakdown and infection, especially if the patient has undergone
preoperative radiation therapy. (Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant soft-tissue tumors, in
Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1605-1618.)
Outcomes
The combination of radiation therapy and surgical management minimizes the risk of local
recurrence to less than 10%.
The most common site of metastasis is the lungs.
Lymph node metastasis (normally <5%) occurs more frequently with rhabdomyosarcoma,
synovial sarcoma, epithelioid sarcoma, clear cell sarcoma, and angiosarcoma.
Tumor stage (localized versus metastatic) is the most crucial factor in determining overall
prognosis/outcome. Other prognostic factors include histologic grade, size, and depth of
tumor.
Tumor grade is related to the risk of metastasis (low grade, <10%; intermediate grade, 10% to
25%; high grade, >50%).
The outcome of individual soft-tissue sarcoma subtypes rarely is reported; approximately 50%
of patients with high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma die of the disease.
Resection of pulmonary metastasis may cure as many as 25% of patients.
Stereotactic body radiation therapy allows for local control of 86% of sarcoma lung metastasis
at 24 months.
Patients require follow-up imaging of the primary site of resection (MRI with/without contrast,
or ultrasonography) and the chest (radiography or CT) every 3 to 4 months for 2 years and
